title: Experiment: decision model comparison at 400 cycles (Jev 1.13.0, gpt-4.1-mini, gpt-4.1)
description:
Pre-registered 2026-10-09 before any run.

Design: the 400-item editorial corpus (sha256 3ce5aacf...), the same seed (editorial-prequential-v1), review everything, empty starting rubric, current gate configuration (the recorded runs' configuration, not the G configuration from decision-flywheel-b1b1827a), optimizer gpt-4.1-mini in every arm. Only the decision model changes:
- Jev 1.13.0 through the Jev adapter (one SDK request per item answering the decision and every discovered element together), list price 0.042 USD per million input tokens (TypeSafe's published price);
- gpt-4.1-mini: the five recorded runs (400-cycle recording v1, attempts 1, 3, 4 and the 412-cycle replicate), no new run;
- gpt-4.1, list price 2.00 input, 0.50 cached input and 8.00 output USD per million tokens (developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-4.1, read 2026-10-09).
One run per new arm; the gpt-4.1-mini arm's spread across its five runs (75 to 83 percent over cycles 201 to 400) is the noise estimate.

Hypotheses:
H1 (stronger model raises the plateau): gpt-4.1's evaluator-only accuracy over cycles 201 to 400 is at least 83 percent, i.e. at least 5 points above gpt-4.1-mini's 78 percent mean, and above gpt-4.1-mini's long-run plateau of 82 percent (attempt 4, cycles 401 to 1,100), which 700 more reviews did not raise.
H2 (Jev): Jev 1.13.0's accuracy over cycles 201 to 400 is within 5 points of gpt-4.1-mini's mean (73 to 83 percent); outside that range in either direction is reported as a difference.
H3 (the cyclotron adds calibration whatever the model): for each model the cyclotron's ECE over cycles 301 to 400 is lower than the raw decision model's.

Reported per arm: accuracy, Brier, ECE and mean confidence by 100-cycle window for the cyclotron and the raw model; whether the cyclotron's label ever differs from the raw model's; rubric and ML-model promotions; the 0.80 rule and least-confident shares in the last window; cost and time. Fixtures in schema 2; results note in docs/experiments on branch exp/decision-model-comparison. Budget: about 5 USD (gpt-4.1 about 3 to 4, Jev under 1).

comments.author: home
comments.text: Added diagnostic, registered before running it (after the gpt-4.1 and Jev runs, whose results did not support H1). The reference labels were generated by gpt-4.1-mini at temperature 0 under a stored rubric (task-2/semantic_v2_label.py) from the title plus up to 4,500 characters of article text; the decision model in the study sees only the item's text field (about 1,000 characters, no title). Ceiling check, no learning, no optimizer: gpt-4.1-mini at temperature 0 with the labeling rubric verbatim, on (a) exactly what the study's decision model sees and (b) title plus that text, over all 400 items. H4: if (a) agrees with the reference labels on at most 88 percent of items, the plateau near 80 percent is largely an input ceiling (the decision model cannot see what the labeler saw), not a learning or model-strength limit. Cost about 0.30 USD.

comments.author: home
comments.text: Results: docs/experiments/decision-model-comparison-20261009.md. Over cycles 201 to 400: gpt-4.1 78 percent (H1 not supported; 4.08 USD, 25 min), Jev 1.13.0 79.5 percent (H2 supported; 0.37 USD, 7 min, 80 percent in the first window with no rubric), gpt-4.1-mini mean 78 (75 to 83). H3 supported in every run (cyclotron ECE 0.02 to 0.10 against raw 0.14 to 0.32). H4 narrowly not supported: the labeling rubric itself gives 89.0 percent on the study's input and 95.5 percent with the title, which the study never shows the decision model.
